title: A church met in its overseer
sum: Ignatius greets the church of Ephesus with a long string of titles borrowed from Paul's letter to the same church: blessed, chosen before the ages, united in Christ's 'true suffering', by the will 'of Jesus Christ our God' (1:0). Then he thanks them. They heard that a prisoner from Syria was passing through on his way to the beasts in Rome, and they hurried to see him (1:2). In their overseer Onesimus, 'a man of love beyond words', Ignatius says he has received the whole church (1:3).

The chapter shows what Ignatius cares about from the first line: Christ is God and truly suffered; the church is one; and its overseer stands for all of it. It also shows a real journey. The Ephesians sent men to Smyrna to stand by a condemned man.

views.H: Eusebius says Ignatius wrote this letter at Smyrna and that in it 'he mentions Onesimus, its pastor' (Church History 3.36.5). Lake follows Eusebius for the setting and gives the Chronicle's date for the martyrdom, AD 108, noting that modern critics are 'by no means unanimous' about it but tend to place it under Trajan (98-117). The letter itself gives no year.
views.N: The greeting is woven from Ephesians 1: chosen 'before the ages', marked out ahead of time, 'fullness', 'glory'. 'Imitators of God' (1:1) is Ephesians 5:1, and 'the blood of God' recalls Paul's words to the Ephesian elders in Acts 20:28, 'the church of God, which he acquired through his own blood'.
views.C: From the start the overseer is the face of the church: to receive Onesimus is to receive Ephesus. Ignatius never argues for the office here; he assumes it, and asks them to love their overseer and be like him.

echoes: Ephesians 1:3-14; Ephesians 5:1; Acts 20:28; Acts 19:1-41; 2 Timothy 1:6; Philemon 1:10

settings.what: The greeting and thanks for the Ephesian visitors
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.when: In Smyrna, after the Ephesians had sent their overseer Onesimus and four others to meet Ignatius on his way to Rome (1:3-2:1; 21:1)
settings.why: To thank them for their kindness, which Lake says is the 'immediate purpose' of every letter but Romans, and to tie the church to its overseer from the first lines: in Onesimus he has 'received your whole large community' (1:3).
settings.readers: The Ephesian Christians who would hear the letter read when their delegates came home. Some of them had met Ignatius only through these men (2:1, 'Through them I have seen all of you'), and Polycarp later collected the letters, so that other churches read them too (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2).

title: Burrhus may stay
sum: Ignatius names the men who came: the deacon Burrhus, his 'fellow slave', whom he asks to keep with him, and Crocus, 'a living sample of your love', with Euplus and Fronto (2:1). Then he turns their kindness into a call: give glory to Christ by being one, 'submitting to the overseer and the council of elders' (2:2).
This is the first time the three-part order appears in the letter: overseer, council of elders, deacon. Ignatius does not stop to explain it; the Ephesians already have it.

views.H: Burrhus did stay. The letter to the Smyrnaeans, written later from Troas, says Ignatius wrote it 'through Burrhus', whom the Smyrnaeans and Ephesians had sent with him (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1).
views.C: In the New Testament 'overseer' and 'elder' can name the same people (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7). In Ignatius the overseer is one man, and the elders form a council around him. Chapter 5's page gives how the churches read this.

echoes: Colossians 1:7; Colossians 4:7; Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8; 1 Timothy 4:14

title: Only beginning to be a disciple
sum: Ignatius will not give orders like an important man. He is 'bound in the Name', but he is 'not yet complete'; he has 'only made a start at being a disciple', and he needed the Ephesians to rub him down with oil like an athlete before the contest (3:1). Love will not let him keep silent, so he urges them to 'run together with the mind of God'. Jesus Christ is the Father's mind, and the overseers 'appointed throughout the ends of the earth' are in Christ's mind (3:2).
Humility and authority sit side by side. The prisoner calls himself a learner, and in the same breath sets out a chain that runs from the Father through Christ to the overseers.

views.N: 'Not yet complete' echoes Paul: 'I do not mean that I have already got it, or that I have already been made perfect' (Philippians 3:12). The athlete's oil recalls 1 Corinthians 9:24-27.
views.C: 'The overseers who are appointed throughout the ends of the earth' assumes that every church has one. Lightfoot quotes the phrase among the Greek letters' 'far stronger expressions' for the office (The Christian Ministry, pages 85-86).

echoes: Philippians 3:12; 1 Corinthians 9:24-27; Acts 5:41

settings.what: A call to one mind with the overseer, in the picture of a choir
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.when: Written from Smyrna while Ignatius was held there under guard
settings.why: To press the Ephesians toward unity with their overseer without lording it over them: he speaks 'as people who learn alongside me' (3:1), and he praises them for doing already what he asks ('as you already do', 4:1).
settings.readers: The Ephesians, whom Ignatius praises as already in harmony; Onesimus himself had told him there was no division among them (6:2).

title: One choir, one song
sum: Ignatius pictures the church as music. The council of elders is fitted to the overseer as strings are to a lyre, and in their harmony 'Jesus Christ is sung' (4:1). Each member should join the choir, take 'God's pitch' and sing with one voice through Jesus Christ to the Father, who will hear them and know them as 'members of his Son' (4:2).
The picture makes unity a matter of harmony, not of everyone singing the same note. A choir has many voices; what it needs is one key and one song.

views.N: 'Members of his Son' is Paul's body picture (1 Corinthians 12:27; Ephesians 1:23). Singing 'with one voice' recalls Romans 15:6, 'so that in one accord and with one mouth you give glory to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ'.
views.C: Lightfoot quotes the lyre among Ignatius's pictures of the elders around the overseer (The Christian Ministry, page 87). The music image also says something about worship: the church is most itself when it sings to the Father together.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 12:12-27; Ephesians 1:23; Ephesians 5:19; Romans 15:5-6

title: Within the altar
sum: Ignatius came to know Onesimus in a short time, and he counts the Ephesians blessed for being 'blended with him as the church is with Jesus Christ, and as Jesus Christ is with the Father' (5:1). Then a warning: whoever is not 'within the altar' goes without 'God's bread'. If the prayer of one or two is strong, how much more the prayer of the overseer and the whole church (5:2)! To stay away from the gathering is pride, and 'it is written', in the words of Proverbs as James and 1 Peter quote it: 'God takes his stand against the proud' (5:3).
This chapter and the next hold Ignatius's strongest words on the overseer in this letter. They have been read in very different ways, and the deep section below sets out how.

views.H: The chapter suggests a real problem at Ephesus: some were not coming to the common gathering (Lake's footnote at 5:3 notes 'a curious mixture of tenses' and that Ignatius may be referring to 'some special instance').
views.N: 'God's bread' has the words of John 6:33, which Lake prints in the margin; a margin parallel shows likeness of language, not that Ignatius read John's Gospel. The quotation in 5:3 is Proverbs 3:34 in the Greek form used by James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5, and it is the only place in the letter where Ignatius says 'it is written'.
views.C: The 'altar' is bound up with the gathering around the overseer: in Lake's English of To the Trallians 7, 'He who is within the sanctuary is pure', which means that 'whoever does anything apart from the bishop and the presbytery and the deacons is not pure'. Whether Ignatius also means the table of the Supper is read differently by different churches.

deep.h: How the churches read Ignatius on the overseer
deep.b:
In Ignatius's letters every church named has one overseer (bishop) with a council of elders and deacons under him, and church unity is tied closely to that one man; Lightfoot called him 'the staunchest advocate of episcopacy in the early ages'. How to read this is a long-running debate. The site does not decide it; it gives what the sources opened say.

As apostolic order. The Catechism of the Catholic Church draws on Ignatius for the bishop: 'In the beautiful expression of St. Ignatius of Antioch, the bishop is typos tou Patros: he is like the living image of God the Father' (paragraph 1549, citing To the Trallians 3:1 and To the Magnesians 6:1). It quotes To the Trallians 3:1 on deacons, bishop and presbyters, 'For without them one cannot speak of the Church' (paragraph 1554), next to its teaching that bishops, 'in virtue consequently of the unbroken succession going back to the beginning, are regarded as transmitters of the apostolic line' (paragraph 1555). An Orthodox reference work, The A to Z of the Orthodox Church (Michael Prokurat, Alexander Golitzin and Michael D. Peterson, 2010), says that Ignatius 'stresses the importance of the bishop, the centrality of the Eucharist', and the reality of the Word come in the flesh, and that the three meet at the altar, where Christ's presence confirms, 'indirectly, the importance of the bishop who presides at the altar'.

As a development the last apostles sanctioned. J. B. Lightfoot, an Anglican scholar and bishop, accepted the letters as genuine, but held that 'the episcopate was formed not out of the apostolic order by localisation but out of the presbyteral by elevation': in the New Testament 'bishop' and 'presbyter' named one office, and one elder later rose above the rest (The Christian Ministry, pages 24-25). He did not set this against the apostles. Its 'maturer forms are seen first in those regions where the latest surviving Apostles (more especially St John) fixed their abode, and at a time when its prevalence cannot be dissociated from their influence or their sanction' (page 73), and Ignatius keeps in view 'the same purpose which we may suppose to have influenced the last surviving Apostles in its institution' (page 84). He called Ignatius 'the staunchest advocate of episcopacy in the early ages', said Ignatius 'values the episcopate chiefly as a security for good discipline and harmonious working in the Church', and warned that the language, 'if taken literally', would give the office a 'crushing despotism' (pages 83-88).

Questioned. Calvin, who knew only the long, interpolated form (the short recension was not published until Ussher's edition of 1644, Lake), wrote that 'Nothing can be more nauseating, than the absurdities which have been published under the name of Ignatius' (Institutes 1.13.29). The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1910 described Presbyterians as, 'as a rule', inclined to 'repudiate everything claiming Ignatian authorship'; that is one church's description of another, not a Presbyterian document.

The Protestant answers to the questions themselves, whether bishops are a separate order above elders and whether they succeed the apostles, are on the site's cards at Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 3 (bishops and elders), Philippians 1:1 and Titus 1:5-7, and 2 Timothy 2:2 (succession), beside the Catholic and Orthodox answers.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the silent overseer and the noisy visitors
deep.b: Chapter 6 defends an overseer who keeps silent, and chapters 7 and 9 tell of visiting teachers with 'evil teaching' who 'passed through'. Ignatius praises silence again in 15:1-2, where Christ's own silence is 'worthy of the Father', and in 19:1, where God's mysteries were done 'in God's quiet'. A possible reading (Claude's, not a published claim checked here): some Ephesians compared their quiet overseer unfavorably with fluent traveling teachers, and Ignatius answers by making silence a mark of God himself. The letter never says this outright, so it remains a guess drawn from the order of its themes.

echoes: John 6:33; John 6:51; Matthew 18:19-20; Proverbs 3:34; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5; Hebrews 13:10

settings.what: Unity with the overseer at the altar
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.when: Written from Smyrna, after Ignatius had spent time with Onesimus there (5:1, 'in a short time')
settings.why: To warn against staying away from the church's common gathering: the one who does so 'is already proud' (5:3). Ignatius also guards the standing of a quiet overseer (6:1).
settings.readers: Ephesian Christians, some of whom, it seems, were not coming to the gathering (5:3), and who had heard traveling teachers (9:1). Onesimus had told Ignatius the church was in good order (6:2).
views: Lake's footnote suggests Ignatius may be 'referring to some special instance' in 5:3.
Lightfoot, as Lake reports, took the last verb of 5:3 as a general truth, so the verse need not point to a case.

title: The overseer as the Lord himself
sum: The quieter the overseer, the more he should be respected (6:1). A master's steward is received as the master himself, so 'we ought to look at the overseer as at the Lord himself'. And Onesimus reports good things: the Ephesians all live by the truth, no heresy has a home among them, and they listen only to those who speak truly about Jesus Christ (6:2).
Ignatius's praise softens his warning. He is not scolding a church in disorder; he is urging a healthy church to stay as it is.

views.N: The steward picture is Jesus': 'whoever takes in someone I send takes me in' (John 13:20), and the faithful steward of Luke 12:42.
views.C: This is the line most quoted in the debate over Ignatius and the bishop; see the deep section on chapter 5's page. Read in context, 'as the Lord himself' rests on the steward's role: he is honored because of who sent him.

echoes: John 13:20; Matthew 10:40; Luke 12:42-44; 1 Corinthians 4:1-2

title: The one doctor
sum: Some people carry 'the Name' around while doing things unworthy of God. They are 'rabid dogs that bite on the sly', and their bite is 'hard to heal' (7:1). Against them stands the one doctor, and Ignatius describes him in a chain of balanced pairs: 'both of flesh and of spirit, born and unborn, God in man, in death true life, both from Mary and from God, first able to suffer and then beyond suffering: Jesus Christ our Lord' (7:2).

The verse is one of the most quoted lines Ignatius wrote. It answers teachers who said Christ only seemed to be human and only seemed to suffer. For Ignatius both halves of each pair are true at once.

views.H: Lake's introduction names the error: 'docetism', 'which regarded the sufferings, and in some cases the life, of Jesus as merely an appearance'. The text of the verse varies: Lake prints 'God in man', which he says early church writers quote, while the Greek manuscript and the Latin have 'God come in the flesh' (see the variant).
views.N: The verse gathers New Testament language: 'the Word became flesh' (John 1:14), 'He was made visible in the flesh, proven right in the Spirit' (1 Timothy 3:16), 'from the offspring of David' according to the flesh and Son of God in power (Romans 1:3-4), and the confession of 1 John 4:2 that Jesus Christ came 'in the flesh'.
views.C: Two hundred years later the line was used in the arguments over Arius: Athanasius cited it to show that 'the blessed Ignatius was right in writing that Christ was originate on account of the flesh ... yet unoriginate' (On the Councils 47).

deep.h: Born and unborn: the incarnation in one verse
deep.b:
Ignatius does not explain how Christ can be both God and man; he states both sides and refuses to drop either. Each pair answers a different denial. 'Of flesh' and 'from Mary' answer those who said Christ had no real body. 'Unborn' and 'from God' answer any who would make him only a man. 'First able to suffer and then beyond suffering' puts the cross and the resurrection in order: real suffering first, then the risen life that suffering cannot touch.

Later councils used more exact words for the same faith, and the site's topic The Incarnation follows the thread from John 1:14 through Ignatius. The textual question in the verse, 'God in man' or 'God come in the flesh', does not change this: both readings say that God truly came as a man.

echoes: John 1:14; 1 Timothy 3:16; Romans 1:3-4; 1 John 4:2-3; 2 John 1:7; Mark 2:17; Philippians 3:2

settings.what: Warning against false teachers, and the one doctor
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.when: Written from Smyrna; Ignatius had heard that some teachers with 'evil teaching' had passed through Ephesus (9:1)
settings.why: To arm the Ephesians against teachers who denied that Christ came in the flesh and truly suffered (7:2; Lake: the letters protest 'against the form of heresy called docetism'), and to praise them for not listening (9:1).
settings.readers: Ephesian Christians who had already turned the teachers away ('You stopped your ears', 9:1); the letter confirms them rather than rebukes them.

title: Even the flesh is spiritual
sum: Ignatius is sure the Ephesians will not be tricked: they are 'God's through and through', and while no quarrel is lodged among them they live God's way. He calls himself 'the lowliest of your servants' and offers himself for them (8:1). Then he takes up Paul's contrast of flesh and spirit, and adds a turn of his own: 'even what you do in the flesh is spiritual, for you do everything in Jesus Christ' (8:2).
Against teachers who despised the body, Ignatius holds that life in the body, lived in Christ, is holy.

views.N: Lake's margin gives Romans 8:5 and 8:8: 'People who are in the flesh cannot please God.' Ignatius agrees, but he does not let 'flesh' mean the body as such; in Christ, bodily life is spiritual.
views.C: The word peripsēma, 'scrapings', turned humble self-description into an offering: Lake's footnote says it was used of those whose death was regarded as a sacrifice and later became 'merely a form of epistolary politeness'. Ignatius uses it of himself as one going to die.

echoes: Romans 8:5-9; Galatians 5:16-25; 1 Corinthians 4:13; 1 Corinthians 10:31

title: Stones lifted by the cross
sum: Teachers with evil teaching passed through, but the Ephesians stopped their ears (9:1). Ignatius gives one of his most vivid pictures: they are stones of the Father's temple, carried up to the heights 'by the crane of Jesus Christ, which is the cross, with the Holy Spirit for the rope'; faith is the hoist, and love is the road up to God. They are a procession of 'God-bearers and temple-bearers, Christ-bearers, bearers of holy things', and they love nothing but God alone (9:2).
The picture is the Trinity at work in the building of the church: the Father's temple, the Son's cross, the Spirit's rope.

views.N: The living stones and the growing temple come from 1 Peter 2:5 and Ephesians 2:20-22. Ignatius's addition is the machine: the stones do not climb; they are lifted.
views.H: The '-bearers' of 9:2 share the ending of Ignatius's own name, Theophorus (1:0), and Ephesus was a city devoted to the goddess Artemis (Acts 19:23-35). The spec box below offers a guess about the picture.

echoes: 1 Peter 2:4-5; Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Corinthians 3:9-17; 1 Corinthians 6:19; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Acts 19:23-35

deep.title: Claude's theory: a procession of God-bearers
deep.b: The four '-bearer' words of 9:2 may suggest a religious procession carrying sacred objects, a sight Ephesians knew from the worship of Artemis (Acts 19:27-35). Lake's English ('You are then all fellow travellers, and carry with you God, and the Temple, and Christ, and holiness') reads the words as carrying. If so, Ignatius turns the picture around: the Ephesians are a procession of a different kind, carrying God, his temple and Christ within them. This is Claude's reading, not a claim drawn from a published source.

title: Pray for the others
sum: The church is to pray 'without a break' for the rest of humanity, since they may still repent, and to win them first by deeds (10:1). Ignatius sets out five pairs: against anger, gentleness; against boasting, humility; against insults, prayer; against error, firm faith; against savagery, mildness (10:2). Christians should be the brothers of their enemies, 'imitators of the Lord', competing to be the one who suffers the most wrong (10:3).
Here the prisoner who will die at pagan hands tells the church to love its pagan neighbors.

views.N: 'Pray without a break' is 1 Thessalonians 5:17 word for word. The pairs follow Jesus' teaching on enemies (Matthew 5:38-48) and Paul's 'Pay no one back evil for evil' (Romans 12:17).
views.C: The chapter shows how the church was to live among neighbors who mocked it: no retaliation, prayer for the persecutor, and a life that could be watched. 1 Peter 2:12 gives the same counsel.

echoes: 1 Thessalonians 5:17; 1 Timothy 2:1-4; Matthew 5:38-48; Romans 12:14-21; 1 Peter 2:12; 1 Peter 3:9; Matthew 13:24-30

settings.what: Teaching on how to treat outsiders
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.when: Written from Smyrna, while Ignatius himself was under guard by pagan soldiers
settings.why: To turn the Ephesians outward: the 'rest of humanity' may repent, so the church should pray for them and answer hostility with gentleness.
settings.readers: Christians in a great pagan city whose neighbors could be hostile; Acts 19:23-41 tells of a riot against Paul in the same city.

title: The last times
sum: 'The last times are here' (11:1). Ignatius urges reverent fear of God's patience, so that it does not turn into judgment, and gives a choice: fear the anger to come, or love the grace that is here now, so long as one is found in Christ. He carries his chains as 'the pearls of the spirit', hoping to rise again in them, and prays to be counted among the Christians of Ephesus, 'who have always agreed with the apostles' (11:2).
The chapter joins the end of the world and the end of his own life: both are near, and both call for being found 'in Christ Jesus'.

views.N: 'It is the last hour' (1 John 2:18) and 'At the end of these days' (Hebrews 1:2) show the same sense of living in the final age. God's patience as time for repentance is 2 Peter 3:9.
views.H: Ephesus had known Paul and, by later tradition, John; Ignatius's claim that the Ephesians 'have always agreed with the apostles' looks back on that history. In 12:2 he names Paul.

echoes: 1 John 2:18; Hebrews 1:2; 2 Peter 3:9; Romans 2:4; Philippians 1:13; Ephesians 3:1

settings.what: A call to readiness, and Ignatius's own place beside Paul
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.when: Written from Smyrna, on the road to death in Rome
settings.why: To press the urgency of the hour and to set his own death within the story of the Ephesian church, which had known the apostles and had seen Paul off to danger (Acts 20:17-38).
settings.readers: Ephesians who knew their church's past: Paul had lived among them more than two years (Acts 19:10), and Ignatius expects them to know his letters (12:2).

title: Paul's road
sum: Ignatius knows what he is: condemned, while they have mercy; in danger, while they stand firm (12:1). Ephesus is the road along which martyrs pass on their way to God. Its Christians 'share the mysteries with Paul', holy, given a good witness, blessed; Ignatius prays to be found in Paul's tracks when he reaches God, and he says that Paul remembers them 'in every letter' (12:2).
The chapter shows that Ignatius knew Paul as a writer of letters (his echoes elsewhere point to several of them), and that he saw his own death as following Paul's.

views.H: Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:17-38) on his way to Jerusalem and then Rome is the background. Ignatius takes the same road.
views.N: 'In every letter' is puzzling, since Paul names Ephesus only in some letters (1 Corinthians 15:32; 1 Corinthians 16:8; 1 Timothy 1:3; 2 Timothy 1:18; 2 Timothy 4:12, and the letter to the Ephesians itself). The note on the verse gives the evidence that Ignatius knew several of Paul's letters: the greeting's language from Ephesians 1, and Lake's margin parallels from 1 Corinthians and Romans.

echoes: Acts 20:17-38; Acts 19:10; Ephesians 3:3-9; 1 Corinthians 15:32; 2 Timothy 4:6-8

title: Meet more often
sum: 'So be eager to come together more often for the thanksgiving to God and for his glory' (13:1). When the church gathers in one place often, Satan's powers are pulled down and his ruin undone by the harmony of their faith. Nothing is better than peace, which ends every war in heaven and on earth (13:2).

The thanksgiving here is probably the church's meal of bread and cup (Lake: 'It is probable that there is here an allusion to the Eucharist'). Ignatius sees the church's worship as a battle in the unseen world, won by unity.

views.N: The first Christians 'kept together' (Acts 2:44) and held steadily 'to the breaking of the bread and to the prayers' (Acts 2:42). Paul's 'when you meet together in one place' (1 Corinthians 11:20) uses the same Greek phrase as Ignatius in 13:1 and 5:3.
views.C: How often the church should celebrate the Lord's Supper is a card at Acts 20:7. Ignatius asks for 'more often' and gives his reason: the gathering itself defeats Satan.

echoes: Acts 2:42-47; 1 Corinthians 11:17-26; Hebrews 10:25; Ephesians 6:10-18; Colossians 2:15

settings.what: A call to gather often for the thanksgiving, and on faith and love
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.why: To strengthen the habit of meeting together, which Ignatius links with victory over Satan and with peace, and to remind them that faith shows itself in deeds.
settings.readers: Ephesian Christians, some of whom may have been staying away from the common gathering (see 5:3).

title: Faith the start, love the end
sum: Faith and love are the start and the end of life, and 'when the two come together in unity, they are God' (14:1). No one who claims faith sins, and no one who has love hates. 'The tree shows itself by its fruit': those who claim to be Christ's will be seen by what they do (14:2).
Ignatius insists, like James, that faith is known by its works, and he puts the weight on lasting 'to the end'.

views.N: Lake's margin gives 1 Timothy 1:5 ('the goal of this order is love') and Matthew 12:33 ('You can tell a tree by its fruit'). 'No one who claims faith sins' is as flat as 1 John 3:6, 'Anyone who remains in him does not sin', and Ignatius explains it the same way, by what a life shows (see the note on the words).
views.C: The chapter is pastoral counsel, not a statement on grace and works: Ignatius takes for granted that true faith shows itself in love and deeds, as James 2:14-26 argues.

echoes: 1 Timothy 1:5; Matthew 12:33; Matthew 7:16-20; 1 John 3:6; 1 John 4:8; James 2:14-26; 1 Corinthians 13:13

title: Silence and speech
sum: 'Better to be silent and be something than to talk and be nothing' (15:1). Teaching is good only if the teacher does what he says. Christ is the one Teacher, 'who spoke, and it came to be', and even what he did in silence is worthy of the Father. Whoever truly possesses Jesus' word can hear his quiet too (15:2). Nothing escapes the Lord; let us live as his temples, with him living in us (15:3).
Ignatius returns to the theme of 6:1, the silent overseer, and lifts it to Christ: his words made the world, and his silences were deeds.

views.N: 'He spoke, and it came to be' is the creating word of Psalm 33:9 (and of Judith 16:14, in the books Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include), which John gives to the Word (John 1:3). 'His temples' is 1 Corinthians 3:16.
views.C: The chapter values a life that matches its words over clever speech, a word to the church about its teachers, and about its quiet overseer.

echoes: Psalm 33:9; Psalm 148:5; Judith 16:14; John 1:1-3; Matthew 23:8-10; James 1:22; 1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Corinthians 6:19

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.why: To honor deeds over talk and silence over empty speech, against teachers who talked well (9:1) and in support of the quiet overseer (6:1).
settings.readers: Ephesians who had heard fluent traveling teachers and had a quiet overseer.

title: Those who ruin the faith
sum: 'Do not be deceived, my brothers: those who ruin households will not inherit the kingdom of God' (16:1). If those who did such things in the flesh died, how much worse for one who ruins 'the faith of God, for which Jesus Christ was crucified', by evil teaching. Such a person goes 'into the fire that cannot be put out', and so does anyone who listens to him (16:2).
The warning is the sharpest in the letter, and it falls on the false teacher and on his hearers alike.

views.N: Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 6:9-10, which Ignatius follows in its frame, with 'household-wreckers' in place of Paul's list. 'The fire that cannot be put out' is Mark 9:43.
views.C: For Ignatius false teaching about Christ is not a private opinion: it wrecks God's household, as an adulterer wrecks a family.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 6:9-10; Ephesians 5:5; Galatians 5:19-21; Mark 9:43-48; 2 Peter 2:1

settings.what: Warning against those who ruin the faith
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.why: To make the danger of false teaching plain and to call the Ephesians to the 'knowledge of God, which is Jesus Christ' (17:2).
settings.readers: The same Ephesians who had stopped their ears to the traveling teachers (9:1).

title: Perfume and a foul smell
sum: The Lord received perfumed oil on his head so that he could breathe incorruption on the church. Do not be anointed with the foul smell of the teaching of 'the ruler of this age', who would carry you off from the life set before you (17:1). Why are we not all sensible, since we have received the knowledge of God, which is Jesus Christ (17:2)?
Ignatius reads the anointing at Bethany as a gift to the whole church: the scent poured on Christ spreads to all who belong to him.

views.N: Lake's margin gives Matthew 26:7 and John 12:3. 'The ruler of this age' builds on Paul's 'the rulers of this age' (1 Corinthians 2:6, 8). The scent picture is close to 2 Corinthians 2:14-16.
views.C: The verse speaks of teaching: the church can be 'anointed' with the fragrance of Christ or with the stench of false teaching, and it takes on the smell of what it receives.

echoes: Matthew 26:6-13; Mark 14:3-9; John 12:1-8; 2 Corinthians 2:14-16; 1 Corinthians 2:6-8; John 17:3

title: Our God, carried in the womb
sum: Ignatius's spirit is the 'lowliest servant' of the cross, which is a stumbling block to unbelievers but salvation and eternal life to believers. 'Where is the wise person? Where is the debater?' (18:1). Then a small creed: 'our God, Jesus the Christ, was carried in the womb by Mary, by God's plan, of the seed of David and of the Holy Spirit. He was born and was baptized, so that through his suffering he might purify the water' (18:2).
Every phrase stresses that God's Son truly became human: conceived, carried, born, baptized. Against teachers who said he only seemed to be a man, Ignatius names a mother, an ancestor and a river.

views.N: 18:1 strings together 1 Corinthians 1:18-25. 18:2 joins Romans 1:3 and John 7:42 ('from David's seed') with Luke 1:35 and Matthew 1:20 (conceived by the Holy Spirit).
views.C: The Catholic Encyclopedia lists 'the Incarnation (Ephesians 18)' among the teachings it finds in the letters. The idea that Jesus' baptism made the water holy for Christian baptism appears here early; Lake thinks the reference is to the baptism, not to the cross.

deep.b: John the Baptist asked why Jesus came to him (Matthew 3:14). Ignatius gives an answer: not to be cleansed, but to cleanse the water. Lake renders the phrase 'that by himself submitting he might purify the water', and says in his footnote, 'Or perhaps "by his suffering"; but the allusion seems to be to the Baptism, not to the Passion.' The Greek word is pathos, 'suffering', the word Ignatius uses for the cross in 20:1, so the Plain English Translation keeps 'suffering' and the note gives both readings. The question what Jesus' baptism means for Christian baptism is the card at Matthew 3.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 1:18-25; Galatians 5:11; Romans 1:3-4; John 7:42; 2 Timothy 2:8; Luke 1:35; Matthew 1:18-25; Matthew 3:13-17

settings.what: A creed-like account of Christ's coming, and the three hidden mysteries
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.why: To set out, against teachers who denied Christ's flesh, what the church believes about his birth, baptism and death, and how they overthrew the devil's rule.
settings.readers: Ephesian Christians who knew the Gospel stories of the virgin birth and the star; Ignatius speaks of them as known facts, not as news.

title: The star and the three mysteries
sum: Three mysteries escaped the notice of the ruler of this age: Mary's virginity, her giving birth, and the Lord's death, 'three mysteries to be shouted aloud, which were done in God's quiet' (19:1). They were shown to the world by a star brighter than all others, so new that the sun, moon and stars became its choir (19:2). From then on magic was undone, the old kingdom fell, and 'God was made known in a human way'; all things were stirred, 'because the undoing of death was being prepared' (19:3).
Ignatius retells Christmas as a cosmic event: a secret kept from the devil, then revealed in the sky, ending the reign of evil.

views.N: The star is Matthew's (Matthew 2:2, 9-10); the hidden plan that the rulers did not know is Paul's (1 Corinthians 2:7-8). 'Newness of life' is Romans 6:4.
views.H: Magic was a real part of life in Ephesus; Acts tells of believers there burning their books of magic (Acts 19:18-19). Ignatius says the star broke its power.
views.C: The chapter names Mary's virginity as a fact the Ephesians knew. On whether she remained a virgin afterward, see the card at Matthew 1:25.

deep.h: The star in Matthew and in Ignatius
deep.b:
Matthew's magi say, "We saw his star at its rising, and we have come to bow down to him." (Matthew 2:2), and later 'the star they had seen at its rising was going in front of them. It came and stood above the spot where the child was' (Matthew 2:9). Matthew says nothing about its brightness or about other stars. Ignatius adds both: it outshone all the stars, and the sun, moon and stars became its choir.

Two readings of the passage are possible. It may be Ignatius's own poetic retelling, a hymn on what the star meant: all creation honoring its Maker. Lake's footnote takes the choir as a picture 'from the chorus or choir which gathered round the altar in heathen ceremonial'. Or it may draw on a fuller form of the story that circulated beside Matthew; the letter gives no source, and the site has opened none that settles it. Numbers 24:17, 'A star will march out of Jacob', is an older prophecy of a star, though Ignatius does not cite it.

deep.title: Claude's observation: the star as the first of the three mysteries made known
deep.b: 19:1 says the three mysteries were done 'in God's quiet', and 19:2, as the Plain English Translation reads it, asks how they were then 'shown to the ages'. (Lake and Roberts and Donaldson read 'how was he manifested', of Christ; see the note at 19:2. This observation depends on the plural reading.) The answer is the star. So in Ignatius's order the star is not only a sign of the birth; it is the public announcement of all three hidden things, birth and death included. This links the chapter's silence theme (15:1-2) with its light: God works in quiet, then shows his work openly. This is Claude's reading of the passage's structure, not a claim drawn from a published source.

echoes: Matthew 2:1-12; Numbers 24:17; 1 Corinthians 2:6-8; Ephesians 3:9-10; Romans 6:4; Acts 19:18-20; Hebrews 2:14-15; 1 Corinthians 15:26

title: One bread, the medicine of immortality
sum: Ignatius hopes to write a 'second little book' to explain more of God's plan concerning 'the new man Jesus Christ' (20:1). He will do it above all if the Lord shows him that the Ephesians come together in one faith and in Jesus Christ, 'the Son of Man and Son of God', obeying the overseer and the council of elders, 'breaking one bread, which is the medicine of immortality, the antidote against dying, so that we live in Jesus Christ forever' (20:2).
The letter's two great themes meet in its last teaching: one church around its overseer, and Christ's real flesh, now given in the one bread as the cure for death.

views.H: No genuine second letter to the Ephesians is known. Lake: it was 'either never written, or at all events is not extant in the genuine recension', though a later editor supplied a 'second epistle to the Ephesians' that is 'undoubtedly not genuine'. The Greek of 20:2 is difficult, and Lake thinks it 'not improbably corrupt' (see the variants).
views.N: 'If someone eats from this bread, he will live forever' (John 6:51); 'Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body' (1 Corinthians 10:17). 'Of David's family' according to the flesh is Romans 1:3.
views.C: The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes 20:2 for the Eucharist as the pledge of eternal life (paragraph 1405). Churches that hold the Supper to be a memorial read the 'medicine' as Christ received by faith. The site's cards on the Supper are at Matthew 26:26, John 6 and 1 Corinthians 10; no new card is added here.

deep.h: How the churches read 'the medicine of immortality'
deep.b:
The phrase links two things in Ignatius: the 'one doctor' of 7:2, Christ, and the 'one bread' broken in the church. Ignatius does not explain how the bread heals; he says that it does, and that it gives life 'in Jesus Christ forever'.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church takes up his words for the Eucharist: 'Every time this mystery is celebrated, "the work of our redemption is carried on" and we "break the one bread that provides the medicine of immortality, the antidote for death, and the food that makes us live for ever in Jesus Christ"' (paragraph 1405, citing this verse). A calendar of the Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod says Ignatius 'repeatedly stressed ... the reality of Christ's bodily presence in the Lord's Supper'. The Episcopal Church's commemoration of him quotes him on breaking 'one loaf, which is the medicine of immortality'. Churches that teach the Supper as a memorial or a spiritual feeding by faith read the phrase as a picture of what Christ himself gives, not of a power in the bread. Those differences are set out on the cards at Matthew 26:26 (is Christ present in the bread and wine?), John 6:53-58 (is John 6 about the Supper?) and Hebrews 10 (is it a sacrifice?).

echoes: John 6:48-58; 1 Corinthians 10:16-17; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26; Acts 2:42; Romans 1:3-4; Ephesians 2:15; Ephesians 4:24; Daniel 7:13

settings.what: The promise of a second letter, and the one bread
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.why: To close the teaching of the letter by joining its two themes, unity with the overseer and life in Christ's flesh, in the church's one bread. Later churches have drawn much from the verse: see the deep section below.
settings.readers: The Ephesians who met for the thanksgiving (13:1) and were to obey 'the overseer and the council of elders' and break 'one bread' together (20:2), as Onesimus and the men he brought would report to them.

title: Remember me
sum: Ignatius calls himself 'a life in exchange' for the Ephesians and for those they sent to Smyrna, from where he writes. He gives thanks, sends his love to Polycarp, and asks them to remember him as Jesus Christ remembers them (21:1). Last, he asks prayer for the church in Syria, which he has left in chains, and calls himself 'the last of the faithful there' (21:2).
The letter ends where it began, with gratitude and humility, and with the church of Antioch that he could no longer lead.

views.H: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, was Ignatius's host. He later sent copies of the letters to Philippi (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2). Lake says Ignatius wanted other churches to help his church in Antioch.
views.C: Ignatius's 'life in exchange' is the language of devotion, not a claim to take away sins. 4 Maccabees 17:22 uses the same word of the Maccabean martyrs.

echoes: Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2; 4 Maccabees 17:22; 1 Corinthians 15:8-9; Acts 11:19-26

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church of Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on the way to Rome, writing from Smyrna (21:1)
settings.to: The church at Ephesus in the province of Asia, with its overseer Onesimus, its deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto, who had come to Smyrna to meet him (1:3-2:1)
settings.when: Written from Smyrna, with Polycarp, before Ignatius was taken on toward Troas
settings.why: To ask the Ephesians' prayers for himself and for the church in Syria, which Lake names as one of the aims of all the letters.
settings.readers: The Ephesian church, and its delegates who had come to Smyrna, now about to return home with the letter.
